sources.news_title: Flood-weary US Southwest eyes forecast for more rain ahead
Flash-flood threat continues in the Southwest, but outlook is improving - Regional Media News
sources.text:
Parts of the Southwest could see more flash flooding Sunday after heavy rains caused flooding on Saturday in New Mexico and Colorado.
While the severe storm threat is less today, some storms Sunday afternoon and evening could be strong enough to produce gusty winds, isolated large hail and possible tornadoes.
A large area stretching from western Texas up into southwest Kansas is under a level 2 out of 4 threat Sunday for flooding.
Possible rainfall rates in parts of the Southwest could reach 2 inches per hour later Sunday.
Due to the ground being saturated from consecutive days of heavy rain across the region, the threshold for flash flooding is low for these areas, meaning it wouldn’t take much rain to cause rapid flash flooding.
The flood threat from Western Texas to southwest Kansas is expected to start winding down Monday, but some spotty flooding is still possible.
On Saturday, the San Juan River in New Mexico crested at 21 feet, the highest recorded crest since 1935, causing the river to overflow its banks and flood neighborhoods in Shiprock.
Onshore flow brings high-tide flooding to Southeast coast
In the Southeast, persistent onshore winds are expected to produce gusty winds and coastal flooding on Sunday.
An area of high pressure over the Northeast, combined with a non-tropical low-pressure system in the Atlantic, are creating a corridor of persistent winds blowing onshore over the Southeast coast.
Gusts of 20 to 35 mph are possible along the coast from Sunday to Tuesday.
The blustery conditions, combined with king tides in the area — the highest high tides of the year — have prompted coastal flood alerts through Tuesday from Miami to North Carolina’s Outer Banks.
Southeast Florida, from Port St. Lucie to Miami, is under a level 2 out of 4 flash-flood threat on Sunday.
Minor to moderate flooding is expected to occur during high tide, with major high-tide flooding possible for parts of the Florida and Georgia coasts.
Rough surf, rip currents and waves up to 12 feet are also possible in coastal waters from Florida to the Carolinas through Tuesday.

sources.news_title: More rain expected in southwest Colorado as residents continue to deal with flooding
sources.text:
More rain expected in southwest Colorado as residents continue to deal with flooding
Authorities in southwest Colorado are warning residents that streams and rivers are expected to rise again as another round of rain moves into the area on Sunday. This comes as many residents are already dealing with the effects of this week's catastrophic flooding.
The Animas River remains closed due to hazardous conditions due to swift water. Meanwhile, the Florida River and Pine River are expected to rise throughout the day as water is released by the Lemon and Vallecito Reservoirs.
On Saturday night, parts of Manassa and Guadalupe were evacuated because of flooding. The Volunteer Romeo Fire Department said that, while not every street was underwater, Main Street experienced significant flooding.
The Conejos County Sheriff's Department has been working to contact residents and help people in affected areas. The fire department says road crews and volunteers are using backhoes to help divert the water away from Manassa.
The Colorado Department of Transportation says water flow levels in the San Juan River increased significantly overnight, and the San Juan River Bridge remains closed.
On Saturday, Colorado Emergency Management provided a list of services available to support impacted communities and survivors with shelter, food, basic necessities and cleanup tools/services. Colorado Voluntary Organizations Active in Disaster is working with organizations to help provide disaster resources.
You can find the CEM's list of organizations and resources below.

sources.news_title: Rain and floods and tornadoes, oh my! Another burst of tropical moisture slams the Southwest, and this one’s a real doozy — Jonathan P. Thompson (LandDesk.org)
sources.text:
From Jonathan’s BlueSky feed this morning:
Click the link to read the article on The Land Desk website (Jonathan P. Thompson):
October 23, 2026
Yet another round of storms slammed the Southwest this week, wreaking havoc across the region and hitting the Four Corners Country hard. By Friday morning, the rain had let up in most places, but some rivers are continuing to rise toward flood levels. Here’s a quick rundown of some notable impacts, then on to the hydrographs:
- The Navajo Nation once again suffered major flash flooding that washed out roads or otherwise rendered them impassible. Perhaps the worst of it unfolded in Dennehetso, a low-lying community between Kayenta and Mexican Water, where the Navajo Department of Emergency Management and other agencies had to use a specialized vehicle to rescue 30 people from flooded homes.
- An emergency was declared in Hurricane, Utah, after a couple of inches of rain fell in the headwaters of Gould Wash, which then partially inundated the southwest Utah community.
- An evacuation order was issued for low lying areas along the San Juan River, as stream levels met and then exceeded last October’s high-water levels.
- The Colorado Department of Transportation closed a segment of Hwy 550 over Red Mountain Pass, CO 17 over Cumbres Pass, Hwy 160 over Wolf Creek Pass, CO 151 near Chimney Rock, and a section of Hwy 160 west of Pagosa Springs due to flooding, debris flows, and/or safety concerns. Those segments remained closed as of Friday morning at 8 a.m.
- And in Heber, Arizona, a possible tornado caused widespread damage.
RERUN: Four Corners floods: past, present, and … future? Is this the year for a 1911 repeat? — Jonathan P. Thompson
Now for a look at some streamflows.
While it’s been a bit too warm for this wet stuff to take the form of snow in the lowlands and midlands, it has left a good coating of wet, white stuff on the peaks. The Center for Snow and Avalanche Studies monitor at its Senator Beck Study Plot near Red Mountain Pass is recording 12.8 inches of snow, with about five inches of snow water equivalent. That’s significantly higher than what the nearby SNOTEL station is currently recording (2.8 inches of SWE).
